title: Budget 2027: Treasury says expect reforms push, not tax cuts | Daily FT
summary:
Wednesday, 14 October 2026 00:00
-     - 80

By Devan Daniel

Businesses should not bank on tax cuts in the 2027 Budget, the Treasury has signalled. The Government is instead relying on reforms, digitised tax administration and a World Bank-backed strategy targeting 7% growth to lift the economy.

Treasury Secretary Dr. Harshana Suriyapperuma was speaking yesterday at the Sri Lanka Economic and Investment Summit. He was answering a question on whether the Budget would ease corporate tax, VAT and the Social Security Contribution Levy (SSCL), which businesses say are among the highest in the region and are holding back investment.

“The reason Sri Lanka is at that point is not by choice. As a nation, we were forced to that point because of the reckless way the economy was managed, without foresight or insight,” he said.

Dr. Suriyapperuma said revenue measures were performing as expected and had lifted the revenue-to-GDP ratio from about 7% to 16%. Interest payments, which absorbed 80% of revenue two to three years ago, have fallen to 40% this year. He said the revenue was being returned to the community through welfare payments, the diesel subsidy and Rs. 96 billion in SME lending this year, most of which went to micro, small and medium enterprises.

“As of now, the priority is to allow businesses to stay afloat, succeed, expand and create more jobs. I’m sure that in time to come, it will give us space to re-look at some of the rates that we have now,” he said.

Rather than raising rates, the Government is increasing revenue by improving tax administration. The Act allows the Inland Revenue Department (IRD) up to 45 days to process VAT refunds. Dr. Suriyapperuma said the average is now 29 days, and in the second month of the new system, a refund was processed in a single day because input and output claims are matched automatically.

“We are talking of Rs. 120 billion in additional revenue that we are generating, not by increasing rates, but by improving our processes and systems,” he said. He was referring to a positive cash flow effect of about Rs. 10 billion a month.

He said the IRD had worked to change the perception among businesses that money paid in never came back. The Treasury met business chambers, trade associations and IRD officials monthly for a year, and the IRD cleared a backlog of long-pending refund claims.

On growth, Dr. Suriyapperuma said the Government was working with the World Bank on a strategy for 7% growth. Compounded over the years, this would double the economy from $ 100 billion to $ 200 billion. Per capita income currently stands at about $ 5,000. The strategy includes immediate, short-, medium- and long-term measures.

He said external validation of Sri Lanka’s stability, such as a rating upgrade, mattered more than the Government’s own claims. “No matter how loud we speak for ourselves, it is the validation from independent agencies that Sri Lanka has reached the destination that really matters,” he said.

He described the second pillar as continued reform, through amendments to existing Acts and new Bills to close gaps and reduce leakages. Some Bills have completed the process and will be tabled at the upcoming Cabinet meeting, while others are awaiting responses from the Legal Draftsman’s Department.

The third pillar is implementation. “No matter how many Bills and new regulations we have, at the end of the day, it will boil down to implementation,” he said.

As evidence that implementation is under way, he said Sri Lanka scored 95% on a global trade facilitation index in April, placing it above the global average according to World Trade Organisation data. He added that the Tourist VAT Refund Scheme, which has been running for nearly a year, is working well.

Digital invoicing is also being rolled out in three phases. The first phase, covering exporters, has been completed. The second phase, covering nearly 36,000 VAT-registered suppliers, is now in user testing, and hundreds of businesses volunteered to be among the first cases. Work has also started on the third phase, a full nationwide rollout.

He also cited the SriLankan Airlines restructuring. The airline needed at least 75% creditor acceptance, but received 99%, including from creditors who had taken it to court two months earlier.

Beyond domestic reforms, Dr. Suriyapperuma said the Government’s growth push would focus on connecting SMEs to global value chains. “Instead of businesses trying to serve a market of 20 million locally, we want them to expand and reach the 200 million and 2 billion markets outside Sri Lanka,” he said. He added that competitiveness strategies would be rolled out, some of them in the Budget.

“Reach out to us. We are ready to listen,” he told the business community.

title: Govt. to raise up to  $ 300 m via Domestic Dollar Bonds | Daily FT
summary:
Wednesday, 14 October 2026 00:30
-     - 35

The Government will raise up to $ 300 million through an issue of Domestic Dollar Bonds (DDBs), Treasury Secretary Dr. Harshana Suriyapperuma said yesterday. It is opening the issue to diaspora and individual investors for the first time since the debt crisis.

Speaking at the Sri Lanka Economic and Investment Summit, Dr. Suriyapperuma said the $ 100 million offer could be topped up by another $ 200 million in two tranches.

This is the second US dollar-denominated Bond offer since the debt crisis. In 2025, the Government raised about $ 50 million through a DDB issue with a $ 1 million ticket size, which was aimed mainly at banks. This time, the minimum investment has been cut to $ 10,000 to draw in a much wider pool of investors.

“Last time, the ticket size was $ 1 million because it was open only to commercial banks. This time, it is open to the diaspora, individuals and businesses, Government or otherwise, who have access to foreign earnings and savings,” Dr. Suriyapperuma said.

He described the issue as a test of the local market. He added that it was meant to show the direction the Government is taking to maintain financial stability alongside debt sustainability.

“The targets are very clearly laid out, and we have reached the required levels as of now,” he said.

Dr. Suriyapperuma said the Government’s debt strategy rests on two approaches. The first is to cut interest costs by retiring debt as early as possible. The second is to replace short-term borrowing with long-term borrowing to bring predictability, consistency and stability. The Government is also cutting its exposure to foreign currency debt in favour of rupee debt, a strategy he said had worked well so far.

“We are looking at all options. Not a single option is set aside,” he said. He added that the Treasury would choose whichever route best serves the country’s interest, whether that is the local market or a more open market for investors.

According to the offer document, the Public Debt Management Office (PDMO) of the Finance, Planning and Economic Development Ministry is offering Bonds with maturities of one, two and three years. The fixed interest rates for all three maturities will be set through competitive bidding.

Subscriptions open at 9 a.m. on 19 October, 2026 and close at noon on 23 October, 2026. Settlement is on 30 October, 2026. Larger applications must be in multiples of $ 10,000.

Interest will be paid twice a year, on 30 April and 30 October. It will be calculated on the actual number of days in each period over a 360-day year. Principal and interest will be paid in dollars and can be taken out of the country in full.

The issue is open to foreign citizens and Sri Lankans living abroad investing through Inward Investment Accounts, and to holders of personal and business foreign currency accounts and offshore banking accounts. 

Companies, partnerships and funds established overseas can also invest, as can licensed commercial banks appointed as authorised dealers, and licensed specialised banks and finance companies permitted to accept foreign currency deposits. Because of US regulatory requirements, the Bonds will not be offered, sold or transferred to US persons or within the US.

Applications must be submitted through 15 designated agents, which are selected licensed commercial banks and primary dealers. Bank of Ceylon is the paying agent. The Bonds are being issued under the Public Debt Management Act No. 33 of 2024, and the Central Bank has granted the required permission under the Foreign Exchange Act No. 12 of 2017.

title: PM urges private sector to take risks, invest in skills to stem brain drain | Daily FT
summary:
Wednesday, 14 October 2026 00:26
-     - 30

Prime Minister Dr. Harini Amarasuriya (right) shares a light moment with The Ceylon Chamber of Commerce Chairperson Krishan Balendra at the Sri Lanka Economic and Investment Summit yesterday      - Pic by Ruwan Walpola

By Charumini de Silva 

Prime Minister Dr. Harini Amarasuriya yesterday called on the private sector to take calculated risks, invest in workforce development and help create meaningful employment opportunities at home, warning that the country’s transformation cannot be left to the Government alone.

Addressing the Sri Lanka Economic and Investment Summit 2026 organised by the Ceylon Chamber of Commerce, she urged the businesses to move beyond immediate commercial interests and take greater responsibility for developing the skills and opportunities needed to retain young talent.

“I would ask the private sector to take some calculated risks,” she said, stressing that the Government could neither take all the risks nor carry the entire responsibility for national economic transformation.

Dr. Amarasuriya urged businesses to work with vocational institutes to shape training programmes around industry requirements and, where necessary, invest in initiatives that may not deliver immediate profits but contribute to the country’s longer-term development.

The appeal comes as Sri Lanka seeks to move beyond economic stabilisation towards stronger growth, with the Government positioning digitalisation, technology-driven exports and workforce development as key pillars of the next phase.

“We have talked about our potential for so long. It’s time we actually realised it,” the Prime Minister said, calling for greater ambition and shared responsibility across Government, business and young people.

Outlining the Government’s digital transformation agenda, Dr. Amarasuriya said Sri Lanka was targeting a $ 15 billion digital economy by 2030, alongside $ 5 billion in digital exports and a digital workforce of 200,000 professionals.

Noting that the total exports had exceeded $ 9 billion in the first half of 2026, she said technology and business services continued to demonstrate momentum, highlighting the potential to move beyond reliance on low-cost services towards higher-value innovation.

She said the objective was to transform Sri Lanka from a consumer of technology into a creator of innovation, supported by stronger digital infrastructure, skills and partnerships with international investors.

“Today, our dialogue on nation-building in the digital age goes beyond simply adopting new tools. It is about building a strong, modern economy where everyone can thrive,” she stressed.

The Government had committed around Rs. 30 billion towards foundational digital transformation initiatives, with the Digital Economy Ministry providing a dedicated institutional structure to coordinate the effort.

Dr. Amarasuriya cited GovPay, which had processed over Rs. 6 billion in payments and connected over 300 organisations, as an example of how digital systems could simplify interactions between citizens, businesses and the State.

She said digital public infrastructure should reduce unnecessary physical visits and administrative delays, whilst improving transparency, service delivery and public trust.

The Prime Minister said digital transformation was also being pursued across healthcare, agriculture, energy and transport, with technology expected to improve productivity, access and efficiency.

In healthcare, the Government was advancing digital health frameworks and telemedicine networks, alongside plans for centralised electronic health records to allow authorised clinicians to access patient histories across the country.

In agriculture, it was working with the World Bank and other development partners to explore how technology could raise productivity and improve efficiency.

She also highlighted the role of digital energy management systems and smart grids in balancing variable renewable generation, improving electricity distribution and reducing the risk of power disruptions as demand for digital services expands.

In transport, online railway season ticketing, digital bus fare payments and online seat reservations were cited as examples of relatively simple technologies that could improve convenience. Further integration of digital ticketing, real-time fleet tracking and AI-driven traffic management could help reduce congestion, fuel consumption and uncertainty, she said.

“The Government’s measure of success, should be whether digitalisation makes daily life, public services, healthcare, education and business operations more accessible and convenient, rather than simply counting the number of applications developed,” she pointed out.

Dr. Amarasuriya said infrastructure alone would not deliver the digital economy ambition unless Sri Lanka also invested in people and adapted its education and training systems to changing workplace requirements.

 “We really want to have a conversation with all of you,” she told the business community, urging employers to invest in workforce development as a shared national responsibility rather than focusing only on their immediate recruitment needs.

The Government had also developed a micro-credentials policy to support shorter, flexible learning pathways in fields such as artificial intelligence, cloud computing, cybersecurity and digital finance, enabling workers to upgrade their skills throughout their careers.

The Prime Minister said digital technology could help decentralise economic opportunities by enabling talent in rural areas to access employment and markets without having to relocate to Colombo.

The Government wants to encourage regional technology hubs linking universities, vocational training centres and businesses, allowing more communities to participate in the digital economy.

However, she cautioned that technology would not automatically reduce inequality, warning that poorly managed digital transitions could reproduce existing disparities.

Dr. Amarasuriya said policies therefore had to remain citizen-centred and inclusive, ensuring that the benefits of digitalisation reached people across the country.

title: IMF sees Sri Lanka’s growth easing to 3.7% in 2027 | Daily FT
summary:
Wednesday, 14 October 2026 00:25

The International Monetary Fund (IMF) expects Sri Lanka’s economic growth to moderate to 3.7% in 2027, according to its latest World Economic Outlook.

The IMF forecast comes as the World Bank recently upgraded its outlook for Sri Lanka, raising its 2026 growth forecast to 4.4% from the 3.6% it projected in April. However, it warned that the recovery remains uneven. Poverty is still above pre-crisis levels, and real wages are about 12% below 2019 levels.

The IMF projects inflation of 5.4% and an unemployment rate of 3.9% for 2027.

The forecasts cover the closing stages of Sri Lanka’s IMF Extended Fund Facility (EFF) program which is expected to end in March 2027.

For the world economy, the IMF forecasts growth of 3.1% in 2026, picking up to 3.4% in 2027. It expects global headline inflation to rise to 4.7% this year before easing to 4.1% in 2027. The IMF attributed the rise in inflation to the wars in Ukraine and West Asia, which have driven sharp increases in energy and other commodity prices, and to significant changes in trade barriers.

title: ‘Problem is too few taxpayers, not high taxes’: Dr. Roshan Perera | Daily FT
summary:
Wednesday, 14 October 2026 00:24
-     - 34

Centre for Poverty Analysis Consultant Dr. Roshan Perera

            - Pic by Ruwan Walpola

Sri Lanka’s fiscal problem is not that it taxes too much but that too few people pay taxes, Centre for Poverty Analysis Consultant Dr. Roshan Perera said yesterday. She said the tax-to-GDP ratio must be maintained or raised for growth to be sustained.

“I am going to say something that is not going to be very popular in this room. I think Sri Lanka’s fiscal problem is not that we tax too much. It is that too few people pay tax,” Dr. Perera said, speaking on a panel at the Sri Lanka Economic and Investment Summit.

She said research she had done with colleagues had identified a growth-maximising tax threshold that Sri Lanka has yet to reach. The ratio would therefore have to be maintained for some time to support a sustainable growth rate.

Dr. Perera said household resilience depends on job creation, which in turn requires growth momentum. She stressed that she was not calling for higher rates but for a wider tax base. That would mean bringing employed professionals, property and other under-taxed areas into the net, and gradually phasing out tax holidays.

She also called for spending to be rationalised. Interest now takes up about 46% of revenue, salaries about 21%, and subsidies, transfers and pensions about 23%. Meanwhile, 84% of expenditure is recurrent and only 16% goes to capital spending.

Her research found that each rupee of public investment raises GDP by nearly Rs. 1.50 on impact, and the effect persists. By contrast, recurrent spending has no effect on GDP and is sometimes negative.

“If you want growth that lasts and reaches the bottom half, the Government has to increase spending to build two kinds of capital, both physical capital and human capital,” she said. She added that capital spending should go to carefully selected infrastructure projects that raise productivity and crowd in private investment.

Dr. Perera said Sri Lanka had maintained its primary surplus, the budget balance excluding interest payments, but possibly at the cost of capital spending. Only about 30% of the capital budget had been spent in the first nine months of this year.

She said higher allocations alone would not be enough. She called for reforms in public investment management, project selection based on economic returns and procurement, as well as stronger capacity to implement projects.

title: Renewable energy ambitions hinge on bankable projects, investor confidence: IFC | Daily FT
summary:
Wednesday, 14 October 2026 00:23
-     - 21

Sri Lanka’s ability to attract private investment into renewable energy will depend less on its generation potential than on its capacity to deliver bankable projects, credible contracts and predictable procurement, International Finance Corporation (IFC) Regional Infrastructure Industry Manager for Bangladesh, Sri Lanka and Nepal Edore Onomakpome said.

Addressing the Sri Lanka Economic and Investment Summit 2026, Onomakpome said the country was starting from a position of strength, with near-universal electricity access, a substantial hydropower base, relatively low network losses and renewables accounting for more than half of annual electricity generation.

However, she cautioned that these advantages alone would not be sufficient to attract investment at scale, particularly as Sri Lanka seeks to integrate more wind and solar power while maintaining reliable and affordable electricity supplies.

“The success metric is not the number of entities being created, but whether each entity can plan, contract, recover costs and actually finance its investments,” she said, emphasising the need to translate electricity-sector reforms into commercially credible institutions and projects that investors and lenders can finance.

The challenge, she said, was to move beyond adding generating capacity towards building an entire ecosystem capable of integrating variable renewable energy, modernising transmission and distribution networks, expanding storage and reducing the overall cost of electricity supply.

Comparing Sri Lanka with other Asian markets, Onomakpome said the country performed reasonably well on electricity access, hydropower and network efficiency, but lagged in the depth of procurement, financing structures and the pipeline of projects ready for investment.

“Vietnam offered lessons in scaling up renewable energy and coordinating transmission planning with generation growth,” she said. The Philippines demonstrated the value of transparent competition, bankable contracts and a deeper private-sector generation ecosystem, while Thailand provided examples of predictable procurement, established counterparties and stronger domestic financing.

She said Sri Lanka should selectively adapt these approaches rather than attempt to replicate any one market.

The priority was to combine the country’s renewable energy base and relatively compact electricity system with clearer regulation and more dependable project execution to compete for international capital.

“It’s not a case of one size fits all,” she said, noting that lessons from regional markets needed to be tailored to Sri Lanka’s own circumstances.

Onomakpome identified currency mismatches as a structural obstacle to renewable energy investment, particularly when projects earn revenue in rupees but borrow in US dollars.

The limited availability of long-tenor rupee financing and the size of the domestic banking pool also constrain funding options. Meanwhile, investors can compare opportunities in Sri Lanka with those in larger neighbouring markets, including India.

Regulatory uncertainty, contractual risks and concerns over the financial strength of electricity purchasers can affect the predictability of project cash flows, influencing both borrowing costs and the returns required by equity investors.

She also highlighted a less visible, but critical constraint which is inadequate project preparation before opportunities are offered to the market.

Land availability, environmental and social compliance, permits, grid interconnection and procurement arrangements need to be addressed in advance if projects are to meet the standards expected by lenders and investors.

“We tender projects and then we struggle with actually having these projects financed,” she said, pointing to the gap between launching procurement and ensuring projects can reach financial close.

The implication is that announcing tenders or identifying renewable energy capacity is not enough. Projects must be sufficiently developed, contractually sound and financially structured before investors are approached.

Onomakpome said Sri Lanka had made progress in changing the legal framework and unbundling the electricity sector into separate entities. However, the effectiveness of those reforms would ultimately depend on how the new institutions performed.

She identified four linked priorities: building commercially credible institutions, ensuring transparent and competitive procurement, strengthening grids and storage to accommodate variable renewable energy, and evolving market arrangements through mechanisms such as wheeling, open access and stronger corporate demand.

Over time, interconnection and green electricity products could also expand opportunities beyond the domestic market, she said.

The World Bank Group had approved a program combining green investment, institutional strengthening and a payment-risk guarantee, she noted. The next test would be implementation, including credible contracts, appropriate tariffs, clear rules on curtailment and funded investment plans.

Onomakpome outlined a range of financing and risk-mitigation tools available through the World Bank Group, including project-preparation and advisory support, long-term financing, mobilisation of other lenders, local-currency and blended-finance solutions, political-risk insurance and guarantees.

Payment guarantees can support defined public-sector payment obligations, while political-risk insurance can cover specified non-commercial risks. Local-currency and blended-finance solutions may help address funding gaps where conventional financing is insufficient.

However, she cautioned that such instruments should not be used to compensate for weaknesses in the underlying market.

The priority should be to identify a small number of strategically important transactions, prepare them to standards investors and lenders can trust, and apply risk protection where the market cannot efficiently absorb the exposure, while preserving commercial discipline.

“If we do that, the energy transition can move from security to competitiveness and possibly over time exports,” she said.

By Nisthar Cassim in Orlando, Florida

Leading provider of Industrial AI software IFS yesterday revealed that most companies operate at only 60% of their potential and Artificial Intelligence (AI) can help unlock the balance 40%.

"We often see industrial organisations operating at around 60% of their potential. The missing 40% is already inside the business. It sits in the expertise of the control room, the knowledge of the night shift, and the data spread across every system," IFS CEO Mark Moffat said in his keynote at the opening of the IFS.ai Unleashed 2026, which kicked off yesterday in Orlando, Florida.

"There's more our businesses can do, but we just can't reach it. Missing capacity, missing productivity, the unleveraged expertise – we can feel it. That growth – it sat on the table, waiting to be unlocked, and we just learned to live with the constraints that we had. So, unlocking that potential is the opportunity of our generation, and it is an immediate access to economic growth for our companies. But it's a choice, and you have to take it. You have to run at it. You have to embrace this AI world," Moffat emphasised.

To help companies unlock the balance 40% potential, IFS yesterday launched its latest solution, 'IFS Intelligence', which Moffat said brings all of it together and puts it to work. He said, "Companies who use data in action will be most successful."

"People can ask a question, take action, or hand a task to a digital worker, all within the rules, permissions and approvals that govern their business. That is how the industry closes the gap," the IFS CEO added.

He said that Industrial AI has to be about unlocking some of that potential, getting employees to be more productive, and giving them an enriched job experience.

It was revealed that there will be a proliferation of robotic capacity in the workforce, and at IFS.ai Unleashed 2026, IFS is showcasing 18 robotics use cases.

"All of the data that's been trained on AI today amounts to a petabyte. To visualise a petabyte of data, that's the equivalent of 50 hard drives fitting into one," said Moffat, who added that IFS is bringing new levels of insight and reasoning across that operational data to help companies unlock the remaining 40% potential.

The IFS.ai Unleashed is the premier global gathering for leaders transforming the world's most essential operations. The flagship event over the next 2 days will bring together over 100 sessions covering eight industries and domains, including Aerospace and Defence, Construction and Engineering, Energy, Utilities and Resources, Manufacturing, Telecommunications, and Transportation.

IFS is the leading provider of Industrial AI software, and Sri Lanka also contributes to its success, given IFS's operations here for over 25 years, with over 3,000 of its 7,000 employees globally. IFS has operations in over 90 countries. In 2024, IFS marked a $ 1 billion cumulative contribution to Sri Lanka, which accounts for 60% of IFS's research and development capabilities and 80% of its worldwide product support.

IFS delivered 25% year-on-year Annual Recurring Revenue (ARR) growth in 1H 2026, demonstrating that customers are increasingly adopting and scaling Industrial AI across their operations. The results reflect strong revenue growth, customer expansion, and rising demand for AI-powered solutions that deliver measurable outcomes.

title: Chaaminda Kumarasiri wins CA Business Leader of the Year Award 2026 | Daily FT
summary:
Wednesday, 14 October 2026 00:02
-     - 36

Top professional, Chaaminda Kumarasiri has won the prestigious CA Business Leader of the Year Award 2026 at the recently held CA Sri Lanka National Conference, recognising his transformational leadership, professional achievements and contribution to entrepreneurship and society.

Presented by the Institute of Chartered Accountants of Sri Lanka—CA Sri Lanka, the country’s national accounting body—the award follows a rigorous evaluation of many outstanding candidates. Its criteria encompass leadership and vision, experience in the industry, contribution to the organisation, contribution to the industry and community, achievements and contributions and contribution to the profession.

Kumarasiri’s journey began in an ordinary family in a rural village in the Badulla District. Educated at Walhaputhenna Ananda Central College, he ranked first in the district and fourth island-wide in the Commerce stream at the G.C.E. Advanced Level examination. He graduated with First-Class Honours in Accountancy from the University of Sri Jayewardenepura, earning the Gold Medal as his degree program’s most outstanding student, and subsequently received two Gold Medals for his MBA in Finance at the University of Colombo. He is a Fellow of CA Sri Lanka, ACCA-UK, CMA Sri Lanka and AAT Sri Lanka.

His career spans more than 25 years across audit, banking, healthcare, consulting and governance, with senior leadership roles at Ernst & Young in Sri Lanka and New York, HSBC, Phoenix Ogilvy, Lanka Hospitals and Bank of Ceylon.

In 2016, he stepped away from a lucrative and promising corporate career to establish his consulting practice. He believed supporting SMEs and nurturing entrepreneurship offered the most meaningful way to repay the country that had provided him with a free education. That conviction turned personal gratitude into a commitment to helping others build businesses, create livelihoods and expand opportunities.

Through management consulting, corporate training that has empowered more than 1.5 million individuals locally and internationally, and board and committee responsibilities in several listed companies, he has developed mastery in organsational strategy, governance and people development.

A defining test came in 2025. While serving as an Independent Non-Executive Director, Kumarasiri was unanimously appointed Group Managing Director by the Board of The Lanka Hospitals Corporation PLC amid significant leadership and operational turbulence. Several critical senior management positions were simultaneously vacant.

He assumed responsibility for a round-the-clock large healthcare organisation employing more than 2,000 people, with 88 laboratories and over 1,000 collection centres. Its overlapping responsibilities as a listed company, State-Owned Enterprise and highly regulated healthcare institution demanded rigorous governance, regulatory compliance and accountability alongside patient safety and operational continuity.

Stabilsing such an institution would itself have been a substantial achievement. Kumarasiri accomplished it within approximately one month, then led Lanka Hospitals to the highest revenue and operating profit in its history. This exceptional progression from turbulence to record performance came while maintaining uninterrupted operations, enhancing service quality and upholding robust governance and compliance. The hospital also reached significant operational milestones, including recording the highest number of cardiothoracic surgeries in Sri Lanka’s private healthcare sector.

Under his leadership, Lanka Hospitals received LMD’s Healthcare Equipment and Services Sector Award and “Most Awarded Healthcare Company in Sri Lanka” recognition, Gold at the TAGS Awards, joint winner honours at the National Business Excellence Awards, and Silver at the ARC Awards.

He also conceptualised the organisation’s first comprehensive five-year strategic plan through the HEARTS framework. His leadership supported the introduction of LankaLifeLine, a comprehensive private-sector trauma response service; LankaCare, a dedicated home healthcare service; and the Lanka Platinum Circle. Sustainability governance was strengthened through several initiatives including the adoption of SLFRS S1 and S2 Sustainability Disclosure Standards.

His service to the profession includes two terms on CA Sri Lanka’s Governing Council, chairing key committees and taskforces, and five years representing South Asia on the International Federation of Accountants’ (IFAC) International Panel on Accountancy Education. He also served as Chairman of the ACCA Member Network Panel in Sri Lanka and continues contributing as a mentor, lecturer, speaker and author.

His contributions have been recognised through honours including the ACCA National Advocate of the Year Award 2022 and the CMA Sri Lanka Business Excellence Award 2026. 

A prominent contributor to Sri Lanka’s entrepreneurship development ecosystem, Kumarasiri is Founder and President of the Asia Pacific Institute of Money and Entrepreneurship Development. He champions entrepreneurship, SME development and financial literacy, including assistance during the COVID-19 crisis. His contributions extend to national taskforces and committees, including CA Sri Lanka SME Task Force and CMA Sri Lanka SME Development Committee.

Through corporate, professional, academic and national forums; television, radio and digital platforms; and thought leadership articles in national newspapers, leading magazines and journals, he shares his hard-earned knowledge and insights with wider audiences.

The award recognises a career in which achievement carries a wider purpose. Kumarasiri’s journey shows aspiring professionals how education, determination and service can transform humble beginnings into leadership that creates lasting opportunities for others.

title: Sri Lanka EXPO 2027 promoted in Thailand | Daily FT

The Embassy of Sri Lanka in Bangkok organized a “Sri Lanka EXPO 2027 – Promotion and Networking Session” on 7 October 2026 in Bangkok, with the participation of prospective Thai business representatives, investors, buyers, industry stakeholders and journalists.

The session was organised to promote Sri Lanka EXPO 2027, scheduled to be held from 14–17 January 2027 at the BMICH in Colombo, and to encourage greater participation from the Thai business community.

Ambassador of Sri Lanka to Thailand, Wijayanthi Edirisinghe emphasised the importance of further deepening the longstanding economic and commercial partnership between Sri Lanka and Thailand. She invited Thai businesses to make use of Sri Lanka EXPO 2027 as a platform to discover new sourcing opportunities, establish business partnerships and explore investment prospects in Sri Lanka.

The Ambassador highlighted that the Expo would bring together Sri Lankan companies from a diverse range of sectors, providing Thai buyers, investors and business leaders with an opportunity to connect directly with Sri Lankan exporters and industry representatives under one platform.

Minister Counsellor (Commercial) of the Embassy Shiwanthi Abeyrathne, made a comprehensive presentation on Sri Lanka EXPO 2027, covering the Expo’s key sectors, participation and registration procedures, opportunities available to international buyers and investors, and the facilities and benefits offered to overseas participants. The presentation also highlighted Sri Lanka’s strategic geographical position, access to regional markets and its potential as a platform for Thai businesses seeking new sourcing partners, commercial collaborations, investment opportunities and business linkages.

The program featured promotional videos showcasing Sri Lanka EXPO 2027, Sri Lankan products and industries, and the country’s diverse business and investment opportunities, providing participants with an insight into the breadth of opportunities available through the Expo.

The presentations were followed by an interactive business networking session, during which Thai participants had the opportunity to engage directly with the Ambassador and Embassy representatives, exchange views and explore potential areas of cooperation with Sri Lankan businesses. title: From remitters to investors: Sri Lanka needs an  investment engine | Daily FT
summary:
Wednesday, 14 October 2026 00:24
-     - 15

With workers’ remittances exceeding $ 8 billion and fresh equity investment remaining modest despite a recovery in headline foreign investment, Sri Lanka should consider a professionally governed national investment platform to mobilise diaspora and global capital into cash-generating infrastructure and productive assets

Sri Lanka has made considerable progress in restoring macroeconomic stability. The next challenge is more difficult: how do we finance the investment required to move from economic recovery to sustained economic growth?

The country requires substantial long-term capital for energy, ports and logistics, digital infrastructure, water and waste management, agricultural logistics, tourism and export-oriented industries. Historically, much of Sri Lanka’s infrastructure development has depended on government expenditure, sovereign borrowing and development finance. Following the debt crisis, however, the next investment cycle cannot simply recreate the previous borrowing model. Private capital must play a much larger role.

Sri Lanka’s foreign investment performance improved significantly in 2025. According to the Central Bank of Sri Lanka, direct investment liabilities increased to $ 1.044 billion from $ 759 million in 2024. This represents an important recovery.

However, the composition provides important context. Of the $ 1.044 billion recorded by CBSL, $ 352 million represented equity and investment fund shares, while $ 692 million represented debt instruments. Within the equity component, $ 266 million represented reinvested earnings, while $ 85 million represented equity other than reinvested earnings.

This does not diminish the improvement. Reinvestment by existing foreign investors is itself an indication of confidence, while debt funding is a legitimate component of foreign direct investment. But the composition shows that Sri Lanka still needs substantially greater fresh equity and investment into new productive projects.

The Board of Investment provides another perspective. BOI reported $ 1.057 billion of FDI inflows in 2025, an increase of 72% from 2024. Of the 188 companies that infused FDI during the year, 24 were new projects contracted with BOI during 2025. These contributed $ 134 million, or 13% of total FDI inflows, while the remaining $ 923 million came from project expansions and capital infusions into existing operations.

The CBSL and BOI figures should not be treated as identical measures because their coverage and compilation methodologies differ. But both point to the same broader challenge. Sri Lanka’s foreign investment recovery is encouraging, yet substantially greater private capital is required to finance a higher and sustainable growth trajectory.

The $ 8 billion opportunity

Against this background, another foreign exchange flow deserves attention.

Workers’ remittances reached a historic high in 2025. According to CBSL, they amounted to approximately $ 8.076 billion during the year.

These flows should not be directly compared with FDI. Remittances are primarily money earned overseas and transferred to support families and households. They are not investment capital, and the objective should certainly not be to divert them from their existing purpose.

But their scale tells us something important. Sri Lanka has a substantial global community that already maintains a deep financial relationship with the country.

Sri Lankans living and working overseas also hold savings, pensions, investment portfolios and businesses. Many possess professional expertise and international networks that could contribute to the country’s development.

The opportunity is therefore not to convert remittances into investment. It is to create a credible mechanism capable of attracting part of the additional savings and investment capital held by Sri Lankans abroad, alongside capital from other international investors.

To illustrate the potential scale, an amount equivalent to just 5% of 2025 remittance flows would represent approximately $ 404 million. At 10%, it would exceed $ 800 million. This is not a proposal to redirect remittances into investment, nor are these figures forecasts or fundraising targets. They simply illustrate the potential significance of diaspora investment relative to Sri Lanka’s current foreign investment flows.

A national investment platform

I previously proposed establishing a government-sponsored Public Infrastructure Fund structured as a foreign-currency investment vehicle capable of mobilising private capital from Sri Lankan expatriates and international investors.


The concept should now be considered more broadly. Sri Lanka could establish a Sri Lanka Growth and Investment Fund, or SLGIF, with infrastructure as its initial investment pillar and the ability to invest selectively in other strategic growth sectors over time.

Its mandate should be to mobilise long-term diaspora, institutional and international private capital and invest it commercially in productive, cash-generating assets capable of generating sustainable investment returns while contributing to economic growth.

This distinction is fundamental. SLGIF should not become another government expenditure fund or a mechanism for financing budget deficits. Investor capital should principally be deployed into identifiable assets with sustainable revenues, measurable cash flows and the capacity to generate commercial returns.

Government should catalyse capital, not provide all of it

Sri Lanka’s fiscal circumstances make this model particularly relevant. The Government does not need to provide billions of dollars in cash to establish such an institution.

It could provide limited seed capital and, subject to proper valuation, governance and legal safeguards, potentially contribute selected commercially viable state assets or project rights. That commitment could then be used to attract diaspora capital, domestic institutional investors, development finance institutions, climate funds, international infrastructure investors, banks, pension and insurance funds and strategic investors.

The contribution of state assets is politically sensitive in Sri Lanka and should be approached on that basis. What is proposed here is not privatisation under another name. Assets would be transferred at independently assessed value into an institution in which the State retains an appropriate economic interest. Any subsequent realisation should be governed by transparent rules established at the outset, with the objective of preserving and recycling capital for productive investment rather than financing recurrent government expenditure.

The objective should be to move away from a model where the Government principally borrows and builds towards one where limited public resources mobilise substantially larger pools of private capital.

Government capital should be catalytic rather than dominant.

Invest in assets that generate cash

A fundamental investment principle of SLGIF should be that capital is primarily deployed into cash-generating assets.

Infrastructure should remain the first major investment pillar, but a project should not qualify merely because it is nationally important. It should have identifiable and sustainable revenues capable of supporting an appropriate commercial return.

Renewable energy projects with contracted revenues, ports and logistics facilities generating user charges, warehouses and cold-chain infrastructure producing rental and service income, digital infrastructure supported by contracted revenues, commercially structured waste and water projects and selected tourism assets are examples.

Where commercially appropriate, preference should be given to assets generating foreign-currency revenues or possessing a natural relationship with foreign-currency earnings. Ports, export logistics, tourism and export-oriented businesses could provide examples, particularly when the original investment capital is raised in US dollars.

Depending on the asset, SLGIF could invest through equity, infrastructure debt, bonds and other appropriately structured instruments. Credit enhancement and blended finance could also help viable projects attract additional private capital.

The distinction between a nationally desirable project and a commercially investable project must remain clear. Some socially important infrastructure will require direct government expenditure. SLGIF should not disguise such expenditure as commercial investment.

The objective should be straightforward: invest in productive assets, generate cash returns, distribute appropriate returns to investors and recycle capital into the next generation of investments.

Capital alone will not solve the problem

Sri Lanka frequently treats infrastructure financing as a search for money. But investors cannot finance a project simply because the country needs it.

Projects require credible feasibility studies, regulatory approvals, realistic financial projections, identifiable revenue streams, appropriate risk allocation and competent sponsors and operators.

A Project Preparation Facility should therefore operate alongside SLGIF to identify suitable projects, undertake feasibility work, support technical preparation and financial structuring and convert national development priorities into commercially bankable investment opportunities.

Sri Lanka ultimately needs a pipeline of projects capable of withstanding commercial investment scrutiny. This is how infrastructure moves from being principally a government expenditure item towards becoming an investable asset class.

The biggest challenge is trust

Creating the Fund may be the easier part. Convincing Sri Lankans overseas to invest will be much harder.

Diaspora investors will want to know who controls their money, who selects investments, whether political authorities can influence decisions, what happens following a change of Government, who safeguards the assets, who audits the Fund and whether capital and returns can be repatriated.

These questions cannot be answered simply by appealing to patriotism. Patriotism may create interest, but investment discipline will determine whether the capital actually comes.

There is also a recent history that any serious investment proposition must acknowledge. Sri Lanka defaulted on its external public debt in 2022. International investors considering a new long-term commitment will inevitably assess that experience when considering sovereign, currency and repatriation risk.

The answer should be structural rather than promotional. SLGIF should not simply become another form of sovereign borrowing. Investor capital should be deployed into identifiable cash-generating operating assets, appropriately ring-fenced through professionally governed fund and project structures. Returns should principally arise from the revenues generated by those assets rather than future government borrowing or recurrent Treasury funding.

This would not eliminate Sri Lanka country, currency or regulatory risk, but it would create a fundamentally different investment proposition from simply lending to the State.

Institutional independence should therefore be built into SLGIF from inception. Consideration should be given to establishing it through specific legislation defining its mandate, governance, investment powers, reporting requirements and independence.

Its Board should include qualified independent professionals with experience in investment management, infrastructure, banking, law and risk, including appropriate representation from experienced professionals within the global Sri Lankan diaspora. Professional management, rather than political authorities, should make individual investment decisions.

The supporting architecture should be equally concrete. Fund assets and investor monies should be held or overseen by an independent custodian or trustee, while underlying infrastructure assets should sit within clearly defined project structures. The Fund should be subject to annual independent audit, third-party valuations and scheduled investor reporting.

The principle is straightforward. Government establishes the institution, professionals manage it, independent institutions safeguard the assets and investors measure its performance.

Currency risk cannot be ignored

There is another issue that could determine whether SLGIF succeeds or fails: currency depreciation.

An overseas investor may invest $ 100,000 into a Sri Lankan asset and receive an attractive return in rupees. But if the rupee depreciates substantially, much of that return can disappear when proceeds are converted back into dollars.

For an international investor, therefore, the relevant measure is not simply the return generated in rupees. It is the return after currency movements.

SLGIF should have a formal foreign exchange risk management framework from inception. Natural hedges should be the first line of defence, particularly investments generating foreign-currency or foreign-currency-linked revenues. But many domestic infrastructure projects will predominantly generate rupee revenues.

For these investments, a market-based hedging mechanism should be explored.

The Central Bank of Sri Lanka could play an enabling role, together with licensed commercial banks, in facilitating longer-term USD/LKR swap or forward arrangements for qualifying foreign-currency investment into productive assets.

There is policy precedent for such an approach. In 2021, CBSL announced a zero-cost swap facility to hedge foreign exchange risk associated with qualifying private-sector offshore borrowing. The circumstances were different, but the precedent demonstrates that such a mechanism has previously been contemplated by CBSL.

A similar principle deserves examination for long-term diaspora and institutional investment through SLGIF.

This does not mean CBSL should guarantee an exchange rate indefinitely, nor should the State assume unlimited foreign exchange liabilities. Any mechanism must be commercially priced, prudently managed and consistent with monetary policy, reserve management objectives and financial stability.

Currency risk cannot simply be transferred from the investor to CBSL or the taxpayer. Its cost must be transparent and appropriately priced into the investment structure.

But Sri Lanka cannot realistically expect international investors to provide long-term dollar capital while asking them to carry unlimited rupee depreciation risk. Commercial bank swaps and forwards, appropriately designed CBSL-facilitated arrangements, an FX liquidity reserve and natural hedging through foreign-currency-generating investments could form part of the solution.

Currency confidence is part of investment confidence.

Learning from other countries

Sri Lanka does not need to invent the entire model.

Bangladesh’s Infrastructure Development Company Limited, IDCOL, demonstrates how a specialised institution can support private-sector infrastructure and renewable energy investment. India’s India Infrastructure Finance Company Limited, IIFCL, demonstrates the role of specialised infrastructure financing and mechanisms such as credit enhancement. Colombia’s Financiera de Desarrollo Nacional, FDN, provides another example of combining infrastructure finance with project structuring and institutional capital mobilisation.

At a fundamentally different scale, Saudi Arabia’s Public Investment Fund demonstrates one relevant institutional principle: a professionally managed national investment institution can be used strategically to support infrastructure, new industries and economic transformation.

The difference is important. Saudi Arabia deploys accumulated sovereign wealth; Sri Lanka must first mobilise capital it does not yet have. The lesson for Sri Lanka is therefore institutional, not financial.

Start small and build credibility

Sri Lanka should resist the temptation to announce a multibillion-dollar fund before the institutional framework and investment pipeline exist.

The first priorities are governance, professional management, currency risk management and a credible pipeline of bankable investments.

SLGIF could begin with a limited number of high-quality projects, potentially alongside established development finance institutions and private investors. Renewable energy, ports and logistics, digital infrastructure, cold-chain and agricultural logistics, waste management and selected tourism infrastructure could provide potential starting points.

The first investments must demonstrate commercially acceptable returns, sustainable cash flows and measurable economic impact.

If those investments perform, investors receive expected distributions and overseas investors can repatriate their capital, the Fund will develop something more valuable than any promotional campaign: a credible track record.

Once that credibility is established, the Fund can scale.

From remitters to investors

Sri Lanka’s global community already makes an extraordinary contribution to the economy. In 2025 alone, workers’ remittances of more than $ 8 billion were several times larger than the country’s foreign direct investment inflows. At the same time, official data show that fresh equity inflows and investment into newly contracted projects remain relatively modest.

These are different economic flows and should not be presented as substitutes. But together they demonstrate both the scale of Sri Lanka’s economic relationship with its overseas community and the need to broaden the country’s sources of productive investment capital.

We have spent years developing mechanisms through which Sri Lankans overseas can send money home. The next challenge is to create credible mechanisms through which they can invest money at home.

But they should not be asked to invest merely because they are Sri Lankan. They should be offered professionally structured investments in productive, cash-generating assets, supported by transparent governance, identifiable revenue streams, appropriate investor protection and credible mechanisms for managing foreign exchange risk and repatriating income and capital.

If SLGIF can establish that discipline, its appeal should extend beyond the diaspora. Development finance institutions, domestic institutional investors and international investors could participate alongside Sri Lankans overseas.

Sri Lanka’s next infrastructure cycle should not become another sovereign borrowing cycle. It should become an investment cycle in productive assets that generate income, create employment and support economic growth.

The country does not lack investment opportunities, nor is there a shortage of capital globally. What Sri Lanka needs is a credible institutional bridge between the two.

A professionally governed Sri Lanka Growth and Investment Fund, built around cash-generating assets and appropriate protection against currency risk, could be that bridge.

(The author is an investment banker and corporate finance adviser with over three decades of experience in structured finance, capital markets, private equity, mergers and acquisitions and corporate advisory. The views expressed are personal)

title: IMF Seventh Review and moving forward | Daily FT
summary:
Wednesday, 14 October 2026 00:23
-     - 7

President Anura Kumara Dissanayake

The IMF staff led by Evan Papageorgiou visited Sri Lanka and held discussions with the Sri Lankan authorities during their visit to Sri Lanka in September 2026, relating to the seventh review of the IMF’s Extended Fund Facility (EFF). Discussions will continue in the near term toward reaching agreement on parameters and policies needed to conclude the Seventh Review.

Some of the highlights in the statement issued following the visit are as follows:

The inflation rose to 8% y/y in August due to the global oil price shock, expectations are broadly anchored. This means long-term economic forecasts (like inflation or growth) remain stable and close to a central bank’s target, showing little sensitivity to short-term market shocks.

The report also provides following observations:

Decision to seek a bailout from the IMF

It was President Gotabaya Rajapaksa (Gotabaya) who made the official decision to seek a bailout from the IMF in March 2022. He firmly decided on the move in spite of many key members of his own Government advising and resisting going to IMF despite worsening economic conditions in the country. In November 2023, the Supreme Court of Sri Lanka ruled that some of them including Gotabaya were personally responsible for mishandling the economy and specifically cited their deliberate delay in seeking IMF assistance, massive tax cuts, and reckless money printing as direct violations of public trust that led to the nation’s bankruptcy.

The initial delay in approaching the IMF by Gotabaya was driven by internal Government factions who favored relying on bilateral credit lines from countries like India and China.

However, following the decision by President Gotabaya Rajapaksa, Finance Minister Ali Sabry who was appointed shortly after the initial announcement, led the Sri Lankan delegation to Washington D.C. in April 2022 to officially initiate the emergency financial assistance talks. Central Bank Governor Dr. P. Nandalal Weerasinghe, appointed in April 2022, oversaw the historic decision to suspend foreign debt payments (sovereign default), which was a critical prerequisite for structuring the IMF program. 

After Gotabaya Rajapaksa fled the country and resigned amid mass protests in July 2022, Ranil Wickremesinghe took over as president and continued the rigorous negotiations to finalise the $ 3 billion IMF - EFF program.

President Ranil Wickremesinghe (Ranil) implemented a series of stringent legislative acts and fiscal policies aimed at stabilising the economy. The primary acts and policies brought forth during his tenure include:

Key Legislative Acts for structural reform

Fiscal and Monetary policies

Social safety net and trade adjustments

Aswesuma Welfare Scheme: The administration replaced the politicised Samurdhi welfare scheme with Aswesuma, a targeted, data-driven cash transfer system designed to cushion poorest segments against severe subsidy cuts and high living costs. (The Aswesuma Welfare Benefit Scheme was officially implemented on July 1, 2023.

While the nationwide identification, screening, and application process for vulnerable families initially began in August 2022, the program formally launched and began its direct bank account credit system to replace the old Samurdhi program starting with the July 2023 financial cycle.

Ranil’s structural and financial reforms shifted Sri Lanka from bankruptcy and severe shortages toward macroeconomic stabilisation. Inflation plummeted from a historic peak of nearly 70% in September 2022 to stable single digits—hovering around 8% in late 2026. His administration successfully negotiated agreements to restructure roughly $25 billion in foreign debt with major bilateral lenders (such as India, Japan, and China) and private bondholders, pulling the country out of default. After shrinking by 7.3% in 2022, the economy stabilised, registering a 5% GDP growth rate in 2024 and maintaining consistent quarterly expansions.

He gave full backing to few young ministers from Gotabaya regime and deployed them to assist him in his effort in putting the derailed economy back on track. The introduction of systems like the QR-code fuel rationing successfully ended the kilometers-long queues for fuel, gas, and medicine, restoring a baseline of daily normalcy.

High income tax regime

While inflation stopped rising rapidly, actual prices remained locked at extremely high post-crisis levels. Massive tax hikes and utility price increases squeezed the middle class and lowered purchasing power. According to data monitored by the World Bank, despite macroeconomic stabilisation, poverty levels remained elevated at around 33%, highlighting that top-level economic numbers have been slow to translate into improved conditions for ordinary households. The combination of heavy income taxes and reduced domestic purchasing power prompted a massive wave of professionals—including doctors, engineers, and IT specialists—to leave the country.

Many criticised Ranil for using harsh crackdowns to suppress protests and for delaying local Government elections during his tenure, prioritising state stabilisation over political dissent.

These challenges and negative impacts cost him the top job in the last Presidential elections held on 21 September  2024. People decided to elect Anura Kumara Dissanayake (AKD) of the National People’s Power (NPP) as the 10th Executive President of Sri Lanka.

A Bachelor of Science (BSc) in Physical Science, specialising in Physics, knows Newton’s Laws and continued with the reforms brought about by Ranil and the IMF program.

This is the first time in Sri Lanka’s political history that three different leaders have continued the economic policies of previous Governments. All indications are that NPP Government will continue with Open Economy introduced by J.R. Jayewardene Government in 1977.

AKD was prudent enough to retain two key officials,  Finance Ministry and Treasury Secretary Mahinda Siriwardana, and Central Bank Governor Dr. Nandalal Weerasinghe, to ensure a seamless continuation of the IMF’s - EFF program and to reassure international financial markets. Siriwardana served under the new administration until his planned retirement at the end of June 2025. Upon his departure, AKD publicly praised Siriwardana for his critical role in navigating the economic crisis, rebuilding the country’s tax system, and spearheading difficult institutional reforms.

Past experience

Successive governments in Sri Lanka have frequently reversed the economic and social policies of their predecessors. This lack of political consensus and constant policy flipping has been a primary driver of structural instability, ultimately culminating in the historic 2022 sovereign debt default.

All key legislative acts for structural reform and fiscal and monetary policies, established on the advice of the IMF, would ensure continuity, as future Governments are legally bound to follow them unless amended by Parliament.

Those Sri Lankan citizens who are perceived to be objective, just, and unswayed by extreme partisanship, corruption, or ethnic and religious bias would embrace the changes that took place with IMF assistance without hesitation.

Safeguarding macroeconomic stability

According to IMF report published it was mentioned, 

“However, Sri Lanka continues to face downside risks from uncertainty over the duration and intensity of the Middle East war, global trade policy, and the impact of El Niño. Safeguarding macroeconomic stability in a shock-prone environment requires continuing with prudent policies and bold reforms to protect the hard-won gains of the program.”

The Government has however indicated it will formulate the 2027 Budget (scheduled for presentation on 12 November) within strict IMF guardrails, balancing fiscal discipline with targeted social relief.

“There Is a long way for us to go” but there is a silver lining in the horizon

Economic Development Deputy Minister Nishantha Jayaweera said in Parliament that Sri Lanka has imported more than 800,000 vehicles worth around $3. 8 billion since vehicle import restrictions were lifted in 2024. The surge in imports followed the phased lifting of restrictions originally imposed during the 2020 economic crisis. EconomyNext highlights that vehicle imports generated over 904 billion rupees in tax revenues during 2025 alone, far exceeding initial Government expectations. These figures indicate how people were starved for vehicles.

This also suggests that the country’s severe foreign currency shortage has eased enough since the 2022 default to allow normal trade flows to resume.

Some may criticise allowing vehicle imports because they directly drive high retail consumer spending, but in the same period the country has imported over $ 4.5 billion in machinery and investment equipment since 2024, marking a critical return of private and public sector infrastructure spending.

Capital goods imports are primarily for automated looms and fabric-processing units to sustain the island’s premier export engine, the Textile and Garment Industry, and for goods needed to restart delayed civil engineering projects, including heavy equipment, building materials, and components and tooling machinery required for local industrial value chains.

Bringing in modern industrial equipment signals those local manufacturers are upgrading and automating their production lines. This directly increases output per worker, lowers operating costs, and improves factory efficiency. The results are already visible, with industrial activity expanding by 7.3% and manufacturing rising by 3.2%, partly driven by machinery deployment.

Capital imports are also critical to achieving the National Export Development Plan 2026–2030, which targets total export earnings of $20 billion by expanding the capacity of the top export sectors launched by the Export Development Board (EDB).

Another positive development is the addition of 1,513 megawatts (MW) of solar power to the national grid between 2025 and August 2026 alone. If Sri Lanka can significantly accelerate its transition to clean energy through solar and wind, the fuel import bill could be drastically reduced and even provide free electricity to households, improving the standard of living for our people.
